passage:
Looking back, the numbers were never as frightening as the secret. For a year I paid my credit card minimum and two EMIs and told my family my salary was "tight but fine". At dinner I laughed in the right places and felt like a stranger.

One Sunday I finally wrote every due on paper: the card, the phone EMI, the two-wheeler EMI, with the interest beside each. The card's interest was the highest, so that became the first target.

Then I told my sister Ira. She was quiet for a second and said, "Show me the list." She didn't lecture. She sat with me while I called the card company.

The debt didn't vanish, but the loneliness did.

Aadhya

qa.a: Aadhya told them it was "tight but fine".

qa.q: Why did Aadhya feel like a stranger at dinner?
qa.a: Hiding the EMIs and card dues made Aadhya feel cut off, laughing in the right places while carrying a secret.

qa.q: Which steps made the debt more manageable for Aadhya?
qa.a: Writing every due on paper with its interest, going after the highest-interest card first, and telling one trusted person.

qa.q: What does Ira's reaction suggest about how Ira saw the news?
qa.a: Ira went quiet for a second, asked to see the list and did not lecture, which suggests Ira cared more about helping than blaming.

grounding: Aadhya hides EMIs and card dues from family, then faces the numbers on paper, prioritises the highest interest and tells a trusted person.

passage:
Counsellor's note, workplace wellbeing clinic, Monday.
Charu came in saying she "couldn't breathe properly at night". It emerged that she has three EMIs and two credit card bills she has been hiding from her family for eight months. She had never added them up. She said she avoided opening the bank app.
I asked her to write every debt on paper, with the amount and interest rate. It took twenty minutes. She cried when she saw the total, then said, "At least now I know."
I referred her to the free credit counselling service our company offers, where a qualified counsellor can help her decide which debt to deal with first.
She asked whether she had to tell her parents. I asked if there was one person she trusted. She named her sister, Nikita. She called Nikita from the clinic before leaving.
Follow-up in two weeks.

qa.q: How long had Charu been hiding her debts?
What was Charu feeling before and after adding up the debts?
qa.a: She felt anxious and ashamed, unable to breathe at night, then tearful but relieved to finally know the total.

qa.q: What steps did the counsellor help Charu take?
qa.a: Writing all debts on paper, getting a referral to a qualified credit counsellor to decide what to tackle first, and telling one trusted person, her sister.

qa.q: How might Nikita feel when Charu calls from the clinic?
qa.a: Nikita may be surprised and worried, but probably glad Charu trusted her enough to share it.

grounding: Hiding debts from family deepens the protagonist's isolation; she faces the numbers on paper, gets qualified help and tells one trusted person.

passage:
Joseph's diary, Sunday.
Didn't go to church today. Stayed in bed. Couldn't face anyone asking "how's the new job".
Truth: two credit cards, a phone EMI, and the bike loan. I've been paying minimums and hiding the bills from Amma in my backpack. Every time she asks why I look tired, I say work.
This afternoon I finally did what Omkar told me months ago. Wrote every debt on one page. Amount. Interest. Due date.
It's bad. Worse than I thought. But seeing it on paper is weirdly less scary than not knowing.
Called Omkar. He didn't judge. He said his cousin works at a debt-counselling centre that's free, and he'll come with me on Wednesday.
Not telling Amma yet. But I told someone. That's more than yesterday.

qa.q: What did Joseph write on one page?
qa.a: Every debt, with the amount, interest and due date.

qa.q: How did Joseph feel after writing the debts on paper?
qa.a: Joseph felt that it was bad but weirdly less scary, some relief at finally knowing after the shame of hiding it.

qa.q: What steps is Joseph taking to stop the debt growing in secret?
qa.a: Facing the numbers on paper, telling Omkar, and going with him to a free debt-counselling centre.

qa.q: How might Omkar see Joseph's call?
qa.a: Omkar seems relieved and supportive, glad Joseph finally reached out and ready to go with him on Wednesday.

grounding: The protagonist hides EMIs and card dues from family out of shame, then faces the numbers on paper and tells one trusted person.
